title: Wayfinding: A simple concept, a complex process

findings.antecedent: Correct placement, position, and size of signs, maps, and other wayfinding aids
findings.consequent: Efficient flow of people, quick destination reach, minimum confusion and disorientation in built environments (e.g., transport hubs)
findings.quote: if people are able to find their way in a built environment in an efficient manner due to the correct placement, position and size of signs, maps and other wayfinding aides, then the flow of people during peak periods in places such as train and bus stations, airports and malls will be such that they will be able to reach their desired destination as quickly as possible, with minimum confusion and disorientation.

findings.consequent: Design of spaces for quick and efficient wayfinding
findings.quote: If the principles and elements of wayfinding are understood, then spaces can be designed to ensure that this process can be undertaken as quickly and efficiently as possible.

findings.antecedent: Lack of generic airport terminal design and varied locations/operations of critical points (e.g., check-in, security, gates)
findings.consequent: Confusion and disorientation in airport terminals
findings.quote: Airport terminals are often characterized by confusion and disorientation (Arthur & Passini, 1992; Seidel, 1982). The lack of a generic airport terminal design, combined with different locations and operations of critical points such as check-in counters, security screening points and gates can contribute to this.

findings.antecedent: Passenger characteristics (first-time users, unfamiliarity, cultural/language differences, time-constrained, nervous)
findings.consequent: Stressful state for passengers
findings.quote: many passengers are first-time users, others are unfamiliar with the particular airport, some come from different cultural backgrounds, others are unfamiliar with the language used and some are often time-constrained and nervous, all of which can put them into a stressful state (Raubal, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Emergency evacuation combined with wrong directions and poor architectural design
findings.consequent: Escalated stress and confusion, potential for injury or death
findings.quote: If the evacuation of the building is required, stress and confusion levels can escalate and passengers must rely on the correct placement and accuracy of signs and maps in order to be able to evacuate the terminal as quickly as possible. This was not the case in 1996 at Dusseldorf Airport where the deaths that occurred were attributed to the communication of wrong directions and poor architectural design (Raubal, 2001).

findings.consequent: Increased efficiency and effectiveness of public building design for people with disabilities
findings.quote: A better understanding of wayfinding may increase efficiency and effectiveness of the use and design of public buildings and spaces for people with disabilities to allow them to make their way from their current location to a desired destination more easily.

findings.consequent: Frustration, being lost or disoriented
findings.quote: The frustration felt when a person is lost or disoriented due to illegible, missing or incorrect signs is a common experience.

findings.consequent: Facilitated passenger progress and improved satisfaction in airports
findings.quote: airports can best facilitate passenger progress and improve satisfaction by focussing on key elements, one of which was the clarity of signage.

findings.consequent: Tangible business costs (lost staff time, reduced staff concentration, lost business, missed appointments, lawsuits, missed operational targets, injury/death)
findings.quote: The cost associated with being lost is tangible. Lost staff time, reduced staff concentration due to providing directions, lost business, missed appointments or delayed meetings, potential lawsuits due to a lack of accessibility, failure to meet legislative or operational targets such as inbound or outbound passenger processing times and injury or death during an emergency situation are all areas of costs for businesses (Arthur & Passini, 1992; Carpman & Grant, 2002).

findings.antecedent: Design adhering to universal design principles (equitable use, flexibility, simple/intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, appropriate size/space)
findings.consequent: Improved usability, accessibility, safety, efficiency, comfort, and wayfinding
findings.quote: Connell et al. (1997) proposed principles of universal design, outlined in Table 1, in an attempt to guide designers, engineers and architects design environments that are not only functional, but are also conducive to wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Diversity of users (e.g., in transportation hubs)
findings.consequent: Increased complexity of wayfinding
findings.quote: In a setting like a transportation hub, the diversity of users present increases the complexity of wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Formation of a suitable cognitive map of the environment
findings.consequent: Successful spatial orientation
findings.quote: Successful spatial orientation occurs when a person can form a suitable cognitive map of the environment in order to establish their position (Casakin et al., 2000).

findings.consequent: Quick identification of the shortest and most efficient route
findings.quote: Once this orientation has been obtained, the shortest and most efficient route from their current position to a desired destination is quickly identified (Seneviratne & Morrall, 1985; Ueberschaer, 1971).

findings.antecedent: Implicit strategies (e.g., least angle, initial segment, fewest landmarks/turns)
findings.consequent: Route choice and minimized mental/physical effort
findings.quote: Route choice is affected by implicit strategies that minimize the mental and physical efforts involved in moving through the environment when there is no obvious correct decision (Christenfeld, 1995; Conroy Dalton, 2003; Hochmair & Karlsson, 2005; Hölscher, Meilinger, Vrachliotis, Brösamle, & Knauff, 2006; Seneviratne & Morrall, 1985; Wiener & Mallot, 2003; Wiener, Schnee, & Mallot, 2004).

findings.consequent: Selection of relatively inefficient routes
findings.quote: Sometimes, due to people's different preferences, a strategy is chosen even if it results in selecting a relatively inefficient route (Brunyé et al., 2010).

findings.consequent: Successful spatial orientation
findings.quote: Successfully obtaining spatial orientation depends on a person's spatial ability (Lawton, 2010).

findings.consequent: Ability to form spatial orientation and undertake successful wayfinding
findings.quote: Additionally, the language used to communicate directions impacts on a person's ability to successfully form spatial orientation, and hence undertake successful wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Impaired spatial orientation and wayfinding errors
findings.quote: Using verbal directions instead of or in addition to maps can cause the formation of spatial orientation, and hence wayfinding to go awry (Allen et al., 2004).

findings.antecedent: Culture and social situation of an individual
findings.consequent: Spatial decision-making and wayfinding
findings.quote: Spatial decision-making and wayfinding are impacted by the cultural and social situation of an individual.

findings.antecedent: Cultural/linguistic differences (vocabulary, terminology, geographical style, cultural meaning of terms, conversation style)
findings.consequent: Cognitive mapping and spatial cognition
findings.quote: Differences in vocabulary and terminology, geographical style, cultural meaning of terms and in conversation style (Frank, 2009; Grice, 1989; Lawton & Kallai, 2002; Montello, 1995) also exist.

findings.consequent: Spatial navigation and wayfinding performance
findings.quote: Studies have found that differences exist in male and female spatial navigation and performance (Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Jonasson, 2005; Linn & Petersen, 1985, Tlauka, Brolse, Pomeroy, & Hobbs, 2005), with men usually performing better than women in many spatial activities in wayfinding (Chen, Chang, & Chang, 2009; Contreras, Martínez-Molina, & Santacreu, 2012; Lawton, 2010; Lawton & Kallai, 2002; Malinowski & Gillespie, 2001).

findings.consequent: Greater spatial anxiety
findings.quote: Spatial anxiety is also experienced differently, with women showing greater spatial anxiety than men (Barkley & Dye, 2007; Gabriel, Hong, Chandra, Lonborg, & Barkley, 2011; Lawton & Kallai, 2002; Malinowski & Gillespie, 2001).

findings.consequent: Spatial performance
findings.quote: It has been shown that the spatial performance and the effects of stress are negatively correlated (Quaiser-Pohl, Geiser, & Lehmann, 2006; Titze, Heil, & Jansen, 2008).

findings.consequent: Preference for and reliance on distal cues (e.g., hill lines) for orientation and direction
findings.quote: Men seem to prefer and rely on distal cues such as hill lines that give information on orientation and direction (Barkley & Dye, 2007; Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Fortenbaugh, Chaudhury, Hicks, Hao, & Turano, 2007).

findings.consequent: Dependence on exact pinpoint cues (e.g., landmarks) to identify visual scenes and form spatial orientation
findings.quote: In comparison, women depend on exact pinpoint cues such as landmarks to identify a visual scene and form spatial orientation (Barkley & Dye, 2007; Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Lawton, 2010).

findings.consequent: Increased accuracy in navigating tasks
findings.quote: Men have also shown to be more accurate in navigating tasks when directional information is given (Chai & Jacobs, 2009; Lawton, 2010; Levy, Astur, & Frick, 2005; Postma, Jager, Kessels, Koppeschaar, & van Honk, 2004)

findings.consequent: Better object memory and object-location memory
findings.quote: women have a better object memory and object-location memory than men (Levy et al., 2005).

findings.consequent: Significantly better scores in mental rotation, spatial perception, dynamic spatial ability, and slightly better in spatial visualization tests
findings.quote: Studies have found that males score significantly better in mental rotation, spatial perception tests and dynamic spatial ability (Cherney & Collaer, 2005; Collaer & Hill, 2006; Halpern & Tan, 2001; Jonasson, 2005; Lawton, 2010; Linn & Petersen, 1985; Silverman, Choi, & Peters, 2007; Titze et al., 2008) and only slightly better than females in spatial visualization (Linn & Petersen, 1985).

findings.consequent: Increased performance in navigational tasks
findings.quote: Testosterone levels, or exposure to testosterone, have been shown to increase the performance in navigational tasks (Halpern & Tan, 2001; Jonasson, 2005; Lawton, 2010).

findings.antecedent: Oestrogen levels in women during menstrual cycle phases
findings.consequent: Spatial performance
findings.quote: There are conflicting results on the effect of oestrogen levels in women during the different phases of their menstrual cycle and their spatial performance (Chiarello, McMahon, & Schaefer, 1989; Gabriel et al., 2011; Halpern & Tan, 2001).

findings.consequent: Better performance in spatial tasks
findings.quote: The more pronounced right hemisphere on males is attributed to better performance in spatial tasks as this part of the brain is engaged during spatial processing (McGlone, 1980).

findings.consequent: Easier adaptation to changing route instructions
findings.quote: Women tend to adapt more easily to changing route instructions than men.

findings.antecedent: Instructions given in a relative frame of reference
findings.consequent: Better wayfinding performance, fewer stops and deviations
findings.quote: People perform better at wayfinding tasks when they are given their instructions in a relative frame of reference. More stops and deviations were needed to find a destination when people were given instructions in the absolute reference frame.

findings.consequent: Important role in everyday spatial tasks of wayfinding and navigation
findings.quote: These elements, particularly landmarks, play an important role in the everyday spatial tasks of wayfinding and navigation (Caduff & Timpf, 2006; O'Neill, 1991a; Richter, 2007; Tom & Denis, 2003)

findings.consequent: Vital factors for wayfinding, providing information for orientation, direction, decision-making, and connectivity visualization
findings.quote: communication mechanisms such as maps and signs are also vital factors. These elements are shown in Figure 1, with examples of these elements from airports. Maps and signs are wayfinding devices (Lynch, 1960) that provide information for orientation, direction for decision-making and visualize the connectivity between a current and desired location.

findings.antecedent: Good map design principles (organizes spaces, shows elements without overload, identifies current position, orients map, unambiguous graphics, proportional lettering, sufficient info)
findings.consequent: Improved wayfinding
findings.quote: The elements of good map design, outlined in Table 5 (Apelt, 2008; Hölscher, Büchner, Brösamle, Meilinger, & Strube, 2007; Thorndyke & Hayes-Roth, 1982), include the organization of the environment into clear spaces and ensure that the map remains uncluttered while showing enough information and all the elements of a built environment.

findings.antecedent: Correct positioning, lighting, noticeability, legibility, and orientation of directional/information signs
findings.consequent: Effective directional and information signs
findings.quote: Directional and information signs must be positioned in well-lit places at critical points (such as nodes and decision points), be noticeable and unobstructed, be legible and oriented so that they relate to the actual environment (Apelt, 2008; Tzeng & Huang, 2009).

findings.consequent: User reassurance of correct direction of travel
findings.quote: Reassurance signs signal confirmation to an individual that they are headed in the right direction. These signs should be placed beyond decision points to provide the user reassurance of the correct direction of travel (Fewings, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Consistent design elements (size, colour, lettering, symbols) combined with correct lighting in signage system
findings.consequent: Increased noticeability by users
findings.quote: A good signage system within an environment must use consistent design elements of size, colour, lettering and symbols. When combined with correct lighting, it is more likely to be noticed by users (Fewings, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Grid configurations of cities or city block matrices
findings.consequent: Easier comprehension of the environment
findings.quote: Grid configurations of cities or city block matrices are easier to comprehend (Lynch, 1960).

findings.antecedent: Placement of landmarks at decision points
findings.consequent: Affected cognitive wayfinding strategies and facilitated orientation
findings.quote: The placement of landmarks at decision points affect cognitive wayfinding strategies and facilitate orientation (Lynch, 1960; Richter, 2007).

findings.antecedent: Landmark salience (contrast in attributes, status, or spatial location)
findings.consequent: Effectiveness of the landmark for wayfinding
findings.quote: For a landmark to be salient, it must contrast with the environment in either its attributes (colour, texture, etc.), status (e.g. a church or commercial building) or its spatial location with respect to other objects in the environment (e.g. in the middle of town) (Caduff and Timpf, 2006).

findings.antecedent: Use of landmarks as primary means of providing directions to pedestrians
findings.consequent: Effective direction provision
findings.quote: Landmarks should be used as the primary means of providing directions to pedestrians (May, Ross, Bayer, and Tarkiainen, 2003).

findings.consequent: Calming effect, increased focus on visual/mental tasks, increased awareness, directed people to destination, increased navigability (cool-coloured walls)
findings.quote: Cool colours are calming and help people focus on visual and mental tasks. Cool colours can increase awareness and help direct people to a destination. It has been shown that cool-coloured walls are seen as more navigable (Hidayetoglu, Yildirim, and Akalin, 2012; Stone, 2003).

findings.consequent: Outward focus, increased awareness, easier space perception, effective landmarks for wayfinding
findings.quote: Warm colours focus people outwards and increase their awareness. The use of warm colours allows people to more easily perceive the space and it has been shown that warm colours can be effectively used as landmarks for wayfinding purposes (Hawes, Brunyé, Mahoney, Sullivan, and Aall, 2012; Hidayetoglu et al., 2012; Stone, 2003).

findings.consequent: Affects emotions, memory, perceptual-orientation, problem-solving abilities; low brightness perceived negatively; increased brightness correlated with positive perception of space
findings.quote: Indoor lighting directly effects people's emotions, memory, perceptual-orientation and problem-solving abilities. Spaces with low brightness levels are perceived negatively compared to other brightness levels. Increases in the brightness level of a space positively correlated with positive perception of the space (Hawes et al., 2012; Hidayetoglu et al., 2012; Knez and Kers, 2000).

findings.antecedent: Cool colours and high brightness levels
findings.consequent: Improved spatial orientation
findings.quote: The use of cool colours and high brightness levels help people to be spatially orientated (Hidayetoglu et al., 2012; Hygge and Knez, 2001).

findings.antecedent: Map learning aligned with initial orientation of the map
findings.consequent: Superior wayfinding performance (precise but inflexible representation)
findings.quote: Map learning leads to superior performance only when aligned with the initial orientation of the map. The resulting representation is precise, yet inflexible (Richardson, Montello, and Hegarty, 1999).

findings.antecedent: Access to floor maps in an unfamiliar building
findings.consequent: Improved wayfinding performance and spatial learning
findings.quote: There is mixed evidence regarding the existence of a positive relationship between access to floor maps and an improved wayfinding performance and spatial learning in an unfamiliar building (Hölscher et al., 2007).

findings.consequent: Easier wayfinding
findings.quote: Signage is used to compensate for complex floor plans in order to make wayfinding easier (O'Neill, 1991a).

findings.consequent: Improved wayfinding performance
findings.quote: Signs placed at decision points improve the wayfinding performance (Best, 1970).

findings.consequent: Greatest effect on wayfinding and heavy reliance for decision-making
findings.quote: Direction signage has been shown to have the greatest effect on wayfinding and is relied upon heavily in order to make decisions regarding wayfinding (Tzeng and Huang, 2009).

findings.consequent: Enhanced wayfinding, reduced confusion and stress (but can be ignored or confusing in other cases)
findings.quote: In some settings, signage enhances wayfinding and reduces confusion and stress; however, in other cases, it is ignored or found to be confusing (Seidel, 1982; O'Neill, 1991a).

findings.consequent: More effective in reducing wayfinding errors (wrong turns, backtracks)
findings.quote: Textual signage has been shown to be more effective than graphical signage in reducing wayfinding errors such as wrong turns and backtracks.

findings.consequent: Faster flow of people in a building
findings.quote: Graphic signage though has been shown to allow for a faster flow of people in a building.

findings.consequent: Increased wayfinding difficulty, decreased cognitive map accuracy, increased time to destination, increased wrong turns and backtracking incidents
findings.quote: Increases in the ICD result in an increase in wayfinding difficulty due to the decrease in the accuracy of the cognitive map formed (O'Neill, 1991b). It also increases the mean time to find a destination, the average number of wrong terms and the average number of backtracking incidents.

findings.antecedent: Building's spatial configuration (space syntax measures like integration)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance and spatial learning adaptation
findings.quote: correlations existed between the measures of a building's spatial configuration and indicators of the wayfinding performance (Peponis et al., 1990). [...] travel patterns began to correlate strongly with 'integration' and other space syntax global measures which suggests that spatial learning adapts to the larger organization characteristics of the environment (Haq and Zimring, 2003).

findings.consequent: Different route choices (novices chose more visually connected/integrated paths; experts took hidden routes)
findings.quote: novices chose travel paths that were more visually connected and 'integrated' than the expert travellers who were more likely to take hidden routes (Hölscher, Brosamle, and Vrachliotis, 2010).
